messages.body_plain:
This first snippet demonstrates tickling the bug via plyr.  I can get R to segfault pretty reliably if I use transform instead of mutate in the dlply below.

# Construct a data frame with 10,000 distinct groups, each 10 elements long,
# where a_number is always NA.  (If a_number is not always NA, there is no problem).
library(plyr)
ngroups=10000
tst2<-data.frame(factor1=rep(1:ngroups,10), a_number=NA)
head(tst2)
summary(tst2)
sav <- dlply(tst2, "factor1",
             mutate,  # with mutate, no segfaults
             #transform,   # with transform, R will sometimes segfault in the sapply() below
             min=min(a_number, na.rm=TRUE))

# Some of the results aren't data frames!  The results are different each time.
which(sapply(sav, class) != "data.frame")

But I can't pare down the example to something simpler that doesn't use plyr.  This loop always runs to completion.

# Never breaks
foo<-data.frame(factor1="A",a_number=rep(NA,10))
for(idx in 1:100000) {
  res<-transform(foo, min=min(a_number,na.rm=TRUE))
  if (class(res) != "data.frame") {
    print("Not a data.frame!!!")
    break
  }
}

Is this a known problem?  Is this something I should file in the main R bugzilla?  In my real code, I am able to work around this issue using summarize() and merging the results back into the larger data frame, so I think the problem has to do with how mutate() and transform() work.

so, in retrospect, this was sort of a stupid question to post as it was only matter of breaking the df on the left side of the join into pieces.  For completeness, here's the function I wrote, with maybe the ugliest loop of all time (i'd love to hear an improvement).  It wouldn't work for most of the other join types, however.

build_the_left_join <- function(df1, df2) {
  breaks <- as.integer(seq(from = 1, to = nrow(df1), length.out = nrow(df1)/10000))
  b1 <- breaks[1:(length(breaks)-1)]
  b2 <- breaks[2:length(breaks)]
  y <- NULL
  for (i in length(b1)) {
    x <- left_join(df1 %>% slice(b1[i]:b2[i]), df2)
    y <- bind_rows(y,x)
  }
y
}

Thanks John, this is super helpful. I've managed to reduce the problem
to an error in loop_apply:

library(plyr)
ngroups <- 10000
tst2 <- data.frame(factor1 = rep(1:ngroups, 10), a_number = NA)

pieces <- split(tst2, tst2$factor1)

sav <- plyr:::loop_apply(length(pieces), function(i) {
  piece <- pieces[[i]]
  transform(piece, min = min(a_number, na.rm = TRUE))
})

df <- vapply(sav, is.data.frame, logical(1))
which(!df)

loop_apply() is an internal C++ function:

List loop_apply(int n, Function f) {
  List out(n);

  for(int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    out[i] = f(i + 1);
  }

  return out;
}

That's so simple I don't think I've made an error, so I suspect it's a
problem with PROTECTion in the underlying Rcpp code.  For now, I've
reverted to the old C implementation of this function and it fixes the
problem. You can try it out with
devtools::install_github("hadley/plyr")

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: R bug tickled via plyr?
messages.subject_clean: R bug tickled via plyr?
messages.body_plain:
I looked into this a little bit, and here's my guess -- the Rcpp `Function` class does not properly protect the 'language' objects used when invoking the function.

For example, look here:

https://github.com/RcppCore/Rcpp/blob/master/inst/include/Rcpp/Function.h#L77-L79

An `Rcpp_eval` is called with the unprotected return of `Rf_lang1`. This effectively means that the language object that was used for the function evaluation could be cleaned up, and so any function that tries to do introspection on the arguments passed (`match.call()` and friends) may break.

This same template is used e.g. here:

https://github.com/RcppCore/Rcpp/blob/master/inst/include/Rcpp/generated/Function__operator.h#L33-L36

I think this gets touched by the `eval(substitute(list(...)))` call in `transform.data.frame`, hence the bug seen. And since cleaning up of those nodes is somewhat non-deterministic this bug will be quite hard to repro.

So I believe the solution is to, on the Rcpp side, ensure those `language` objects generated for the evaluation should be protected before evaluating the function.

(Somewhat ironically, this issue is pointed out in adv-r, in a section I contributed parts to: http://adv-r.had.co.nz/C-interface.html#c-pairlists; so it's a little sad that a bug like that languished in Rcpp!)

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm converting my teaching examples over to the readr package's functions. It looks like read_csv can't accept input from either stdin or textConnection. These provide handy ways to put data in the middle of a program so you don't have to worry how students have their paths set. My examples are below. I hope I've made an error or there's a bug in read_csv, but perhaps read_csv just can't work this way as read.csv can.

Thanks,
Bob

+ 2,2,f,2,1,4,1

messages.subject: Equivalent to strip.white in readr
messages.subject_clean: Equivalent to strip.white in readr
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

When using read.csv (etc.) to read a comma- or tab-delimited file that contains character data, I commonly use strip.white=TRUE and na.chars="" (two quotes with nothing between them). That way if someone uses two consecutive delimiters, or any number of blanks between the delimiters, I'll get NAs before I convert the character vector to a factor. Using read_csv or read_tsv I can specify na=" " (single blank) and use a single blank in the data between delimiters, and I'll get the desired NAs. However, in that case two delimiters in a row, or two or more blanks will not generate NAs. I can use a conditional assignment after the fact to set NAs, but is there a way to generate NAs from zero or >=2 blanks in read_csv or read_tsv?

Thanks,
Bob

messages.subject: Example of reading fixed width format data in readr & possible bug
messages.subject_clean: Example of reading fixed width format data in readr & possible bug
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Here's an example of how to use readr's read_fwf function to read data with no delimiters like this:

011f1151
022f2141
031f2243
042 31 3
051m3524
062m5455
071m5344
082m4555

Each variable takes only one column except for the first one, which takes 2. You can specify how wide each variable is using the form below. If you're used to using R's built-in read.fwf function, note that you cannot skip variables by specifying a negative value, but that's easy to work around.

> read_fwf("mydataFWF.txt",
+          fwf_widths( c(2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1) ) )

  X1 X2 X3 X4 X5 X6 X7
1  1  1  f  1  1  5  1
2  2  2  f  2  1  4  1
3  3  1  f  2  2  4  3
4  4  2     3  1 NA  3
5  5  1  m  3  5  2  4
6  6  2  m  5  4  5  5
7  7  1  m  5  3  4  4
8  8  2  m  4  5  5  5

That's handy, but if you get a single width wrong, all the following variables will be wrong too. So it's safer to specify the starting and ending columns for each variable like this:

read_fwf("mydataFWF.txt",
         fwf_positions( c(1,3,4,5,6,7,8),
                        c(2,3,4,5,6,7,8)))

The help file says you can specify variable names using the col_names argument, but either there's a bug or I'm missing something about how to use it:

> read_fwf("mydataFWF.txt",
+          fwf_widths( c(2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1) ),
+          col_names = c("id","workshop","gender","q1","q2","q3","q4") )

Error in read_fwf("mydataFWF.txt", fwf_widths(c(2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)),  :
  unused argument (col_names = c("id", "workshop", "gender", "q1", "q2", "q3", "q4"))

I get the same message using fwf_widths.

Cheers,
Bob

Hi All,

When reading multiple fixed-width-format records per case, you can use read.fwf and give it a list that contains the variable widths. Each component of the list is a vector of variables widths for a given record. The number of components in the list is what tells read.fwf how many records each case has. For example, this file contains 8 lines which I can read as 4 cases:

011f1151
022f2141
031f2243
042 31 3
051m3524
062m5455
071m5344
082m4555

using this read.fwf code:

> read.fwf(
+   file  = "mydataFWF.txt",
+   width = list(c( 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1),
+                c(-2,-1,-1, 1, 1, 1, 1)),
+   col.names  =
+     c("id","workshop", "gender",
+       "q1","q2","q3","q4",
+       "q5","q6","q7","q8"),
+   row.names  = "id",
+   na.strings = "",
+   fill = TRUE,
+   strip.white = TRUE )

  workshop gender q1 q2 q3 q4 q5 q6 q7 q8
1        1      f  1  1  5  1  2  1  4  1

7        1      m  5  3  4  4  4  5  5  5

Error: not compatible with requested type

What am I doing wrong?

Bob

dplyr::%>%
Passes object on left hand side as first argument (or . argument) of function on righthand side.
x %>% f(y) is the same as f(x, y)

y %>% f(x, ., z) is the same as f(x, y, z )

I agree that it is not terribly clear what that does in the help. The object previous to the %>% (or semi-deprecated %.%) is substituted into what is after.

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm just passing along a useful tip about specifying column names in an Excel file. I was using the readxl package's read_excel function to read a spreadsheet that already had column names in the top row. I needed to rename the variables so I thought using the col_names option would be a dandy way to do that. Bad idea! If you specify col_names, then you're telling read_excel that the file does not already have them. So when read_excel is guessing the type of each variable, it sees the unexpected variable names and assumes all the variables must be text. How I noticed this was my date column came out as "42011.412719907406" instead of "2015-01-07 09:54:19 UTC". At first, I went blindly on to specify the col_types argument to fix the date until it finally hit me that providing names was also essentially setting col_names = FALSE.

Cheers,
Bob
